summary: States the problem and requirements for hiding precise location in the emergency calling architecture, where networks give devices location so a call can be routed to the right emergency center. Sometimes the location should not be revealed to every party in the path. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When asking for help, you may need to say where you are, but you may not want every helper along the way to know your exact spot. This discusses how to share just enough.

questions: why don't isps share location data
how can location be kept private in emergency calls
subtitle: Balancing emergency call routing with caller location privacy

tldr.problem: Emergency call routing requires access networks to provide precise location information to route calls to the correct Public Safety Answering Point, but networks and service providers are often unwilling to share location data with all parties in the call path due to technical and business concerns.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines requirements for a solution that allows emergency calls to be routed correctly while ISPs and access providers can withhold precise location information from certain parties, using techniques like location by reference instead of location by value.
tldr.outcome: The document serves as a foundation for protocol design work to balance emergency response needs with provider location privacy concerns.

today: RFC 6444 remains an informational document that shapes the design of emergency services protocols. It established the baseline requirements for location hiding that subsequent RFCs like RFC 6443 (the emergency calling framework) build upon.

sections.title: Emergency Services and Location
sections.content:
The emergency services architecture for Voice over IP (VoIP) calls relies on location information flowing from access networks to endpoints and service providers. This location data serves three critical purposes: routing emergency calls to the correct Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) responsible for that region, dispatching emergency personnel to the correct location, and validating that calls routed to a PSAP URI are indeed going to a legitimate emergency service.

The LoST protocol (Location-to-Service Translation) is used to determine which PSAP handles a particular location and service type. This architecture was developed by the IETF's Emergency Context Resolution with Internet Technology (ECRIT) working group.
sections.eli5: The emergency system needs your location to send help to the right place. A protocol called LoST helps match your location to the right emergency center. But figuring out how to share that information securely is complicated.

sections.title: Why Networks Hide Location
sections.content:
Internet Access Providers (IAPs) and Internet Service Providers (ISPs) typically resist disclosing location information to endpoints or independent Voice Service Providers without compensation. Several technical and business factors drive this decision.

Providers fear that allowing non-emergency access to location data would increase server load and operational costs. Some see location information as a valuable asset and wish to charge for its use. Others worry about privacy risks when disclosing location to unknown third parties. Additionally, many providers lack trust relationships with independent VSPs and do not want to enter business agreements with large numbers of potentially competing services.
sections.eli5: Networks don't want to give out your location data for free or to everyone, because it could cost them money or create privacy problems. They'd rather control who gets that information.

sections.title: Location by Reference as a Solution
sections.content:
Instead of sending location as actual coordinates (location by value), a solution could use location by reference: send an encrypted or authorized reference that the PSAP (and only the PSAP) can resolve using credentials provided by the ISP.

This approach allows PSAPs to obtain precise location information without the ISP revealing coordinates to all parties. The ISP can authenticate and authorize the PSAP to access the reference. The number of potential trust relationships is much smaller than with VSPs, since PSAPs operate in specific geographic regions where only a limited number of ISPs have networks deployed.

However, location by reference cannot be used for the LoST routing step, since LoST itself requires location by value. Also, LoST may be operated by independent parties (including VSPs) that cannot resolve location references.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying "you are at 42 Main Street," you could send a secret code that only emergency responders can open. The network gives emergency centers the key to decode the secret, but not regular people.

sections.title: Requirements for Location Hiding
sections.content:
The RFC defines 21 requirements that any solution must satisfy. Key requirements include: the ISP must be able to withhold precise location from endpoints and VSPs (Req-1), yet the endpoint and VSP must still be able to route emergency calls (Req-2). The PSAP must receive precise location by value (Req-4), even while it is withheld from the caller. The solution must not assume a business relationship between VSP and ISP (Req-5).

The solution must work without requiring the ISP to support SIP or breaking existing protocols like LoST for non-emergency services (Req-9, Req-17, Req-20). Call setup latency must not be significantly increased (Req-13), and the solution must not shift burden onto user agents or non-hiding ISPs (Req-19). The endpoint must be able to discover PSAP addresses and dial strings ahead of the emergency call (Req-14, Req-15).

Additional requirements address deployment complexity: the solution must work with PSAP boundary holes (Req-10), different service boundaries (Req-12), and must not assume Emergency Service Routing Proxies exist at all political boundaries (Req-11). It must also work with IP-to-PSTN gateways (Req-18) and function across jurisdiction boundaries (Req-6).
sections.eli5: Any solution would need to let the network keep location secret from you while making sure emergency centers still get it. It can't slow down emergency calls, break other systems, or make it harder for people or other networks.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC notes that this problem statement does not introduce new security considerations beyond those already discussed in related location configuration work. However, the fundamental tension is inherent: enabling location hiding creates a new privilege boundary where ISPs control what parties can resolve location information, creating both opportunities for access control and risks if that control is compromised.

The document emphasizes that any solution must prevent abuse where fake location information could deceive emergency services or where location by reference could be misused to route calls to the wrong destination.
sections.eli5: Keeping location secret only works if the system can be trusted to give it only to real emergency centers, not to scammers or wrong addresses.
